idiom_name: immutable envelope data class carrying List<Hop> (copy-on-append)
implementation_notes: On the JVM you can lean on Spring Integration's history header unchanged, but the Kotlin-idiomatic realization is an immutable envelope: data class Envelope<T>(val payload: T, val hops: List<Hop> = emptyList()) and each hop is Envelope(payload = payload, hops = hops + Hop(name)) - the mutable header list of the classic structure is replaced by a persistent List and copy(), which makes interception a pure function and prevents branches from sharing state. Serialize hops into the transport's header (Kafka Headers or a framework history header) only at the process boundary.
code_sketch:
data class Hop(val name: String, val at: Instant = Instant.now())
data class Envelope<T>(val payload: T, val hops: List<Hop> = emptyList())

fun <T> Envelope<T>.via(component: String): Envelope<T> =
    copy(hops = hops + Hop(component))     // persistent list: no mutation, no sharing

// at the edge: encode hops into the "history" header of the transport
pitfalls: copy() is shallow: a MutableList hop list is shared between the envelope and its 'copy', so two branches append into each other - keep List and create new instances.
data class equality/hashCode covers the whole hop list, so envelopes with long histories are expensive as map keys or in set lookups; key by payload id instead.
Hop timestamps defaulted with Instant.now() make tests non-deterministic - inject a Clock or pass the timestamp explicitly.
